title: Review an EF Core query that causes N+1 database calls
description: Problem: Review an EF Core query that causes N+1 database calls. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: An EF Core query loads a list of parent entities and then, inside a foreach loop, lazily accesses a navigation property for each one. Each navigation access triggers a separate SQL query. For a list of one hundred orders, the application executes one hundred additional queries—one per order. This is the N+1 query problem. The page loads slowly, the database CPU spikes, and the issue is invisible in local development with small data sets.

items: Understand lazy loading versus eager loading in Entity Framework Core
Learn how the N+1 problem emerges from accessing navigation properties inside a loop
Identify performance symptoms: high database CPU, slow page loads, and query log explosions
Apply Include, ThenInclude, projection, and split queries to eliminate redundant round trips

terms.definition: A performance issue where one query fetches N parent records, and then N additional queries fetch each child record individually.
A pattern where navigation properties are loaded from the database only when accessed, triggering a separate query each time.
A pattern where related data is loaded in advance using Include, resulting in a single query or a controlled number of queries.
An EF Core feature that generates multiple SQL queries for Includes but returns a single result set, avoiding Cartesian explosion.

data.text: N+1 queries are the most common ORM performance bug. They pass unit tests because test data is small. They pass code review because the code looks correct. They only surface in production when the data volume grows. A page that loads fifty orders becomes fifty-one queries. A report that loads ten thousand rows becomes ten thousand and one queries. The database connection pool saturates, and the application times out.

data.title: N+1 scales linearly and badly
data.text: One hundred orders is one hundred extra queries. Ten thousand orders is ten thousand extra queries. The cost is not visible until the data volume crosses a threshold, at which point the application degrades suddenly.

The problematic code loads a collection of entities without including their navigation properties. Inside a foreach loop, it accesses each entity's navigation property, which triggers lazy loading. Because lazy loading is enabled, each access fires a separate SQL query. The developer does not see the extra queries because they happen implicitly.

cards.title: Lazy loading
cards.description: Access navigation properties and load them on demand.
cons: Hard to see in code review

cards.title: Eager loading with Include
cards.description: Load related data in the same query.

cards.title: Split query
cards.description: Load related data in multiple queries but return a single result set.
cons: Multiple round trips to the database

cards.title: Explicit loading
cards.description: Call Entry.Reference or Entry.Collection explicitly when needed.
pros: Full control over when data loads
cons: Still can cause N+1 if used in a loop

data.title: What to look for in EF Core queries
items: foreach loops that access navigation properties after loading a list
ToListAsync or ToArrayAsync followed by property access inside a loop
Missing Include for navigation properties used in the result
Multiple collection Includes that may cause Cartesian explosion
Lazy loading enabled globally without awareness of the N+1 risk

data.title: Use compiled queries for hot paths
data.text: For queries that run frequently, use EF.CompileQuery to pre-compile the LINQ expression tree. This reduces CPU overhead and is especially valuable for queries inside loops or called on every request.

items.question: Is lazy loading always bad?
items.answer: No. Lazy loading is useful for rarely accessed navigation properties or in desktop applications where round-trip cost is low. In server applications processing lists, prefer eager loading or projection.

items.question: What is Cartesian explosion?
items.answer: When Include loads multiple collection navigations, the SQL joins multiply rows. If an order has 3 items and 2 shipments, the join produces 6 rows per order. Use AsSplitQuery to avoid this.

items.question: Should I always use projection?
items.answer: Projection is the most efficient because it loads only the columns you need. Use it for read-heavy APIs and DTOs. Use Include when you need full entity tracking for updates.

items.question: How do I detect N+1 in production?
items.answer: Enable EF Core logging and look for repeated similar queries in a single request. Use MiniProfiler or database query logging to visualize query counts per request.

data.title: Eliminate N+1 queries
data.description: Given an API endpoint that loads a list of blog posts and then accesses each author inside a loop, refactor it to use a single query.
steps: Run the existing endpoint and count the queries with logging enabled
Identify the navigation property access inside the loop
Refactor to use Include or a projection with Select
Run the endpoint again and verify the query count drops to one or two
Add an integration test that asserts the query count stays below a threshold
data.expectedOutcome: The endpoint executes one or two queries regardless of the number of posts. The integration test prevents regression.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: N+1 queries are invisible in small data sets and catastrophic in production
Use Include or Select to load navigation data upfront
Use AsSplitQuery when multiple collections cause Cartesian explosion
Count queries per request in integration tests to catch regressions
data.takeaway: If you see a query inside a loop, you have an N+1 problem. Fix it before the data grows.
